claim: The number of neurons co-expressing Ctip2 and Satb2 progressively increases after birth in the somatosensory cortex.
source: In this study, we show that the number of neurons co-expressing Ctip2 and Satb2, respectively involved in the early specification of subcerebral and callosal projection neurons, progressively increases after birth in the somatosensory cortex.

claim: The mammalian cerebral cortex is tangentially subdivided into several functional areas.
source: The mammalian cerebral cortex is tangentially subdivided into several functional areas allowing effective interactions with the external world by organizing sensory information into a coherent perceptual model of the environment.

claim: All neocortical areas are radially organized into six neuronal layers.

claim: Cortical projection neurons can be subdivided into three major classes: intra-telencephalic neurons, cortico-thalamic neurons, and pyramidal-tract neurons.
source: Cortical projection neurons (PNs) can be subdivided into three major classes: (i) the intra-telencephalic (IT) neurons projecting to ipsilateral and/or, through the corpus callosum, to contralateral regions of the telencephalon (i.e. callosal projection neurons – CPN); (ii) the cortico-thalamic (CT) neurons projecting to different dorsal thalamic nuclei; and (iii) the pyramidal-tract (PT) neurons, also defined as subcerebral projection neurons (SCPN), that innervate different subcerebral targets, such as the striatum, the brainstem, and the spinal cord (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Shepherd, 2013).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to prior literature (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Shepherd, 2013).

evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed electrical differences despite similar morphologies, with citations to relevant literature (Oswald et al., 2013; Staff et al., 2000).

claim: Only a small population of cells maintains the expression of Ctip2 and Satb2 during perinatal stages of corticogenesis.
source: Our time-course analysis of C/S+ neurons confirms that only a small population of cells maintains the expression of these two antithetic factors during perinatal stages of corticogenesis (Baranek et al., 2012; Leone et al., 2014) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analysis data and citations to prior literature (Baranek et al., 2012; Leone et al., 2014).

claim: Competing molecular programs direct the differentiation of major PN classes during late embryonic stages of corticogenesis.
source: This is consistent with the paradigm that competing molecular programs direct the differentiation of major PN classes during late embryonic stages of corticogenesis (reviewed in Greig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review (Greig et al., 2013).

claim: Distinct subpopulations of C/S+ PNs are maintained and gradually increase postnatally in lower layers of the S1 cortex.
source: However, we found that distinct subpopulations of C/S+ PNs are maintained and gradually increase postnatally in lower layers of the S1 cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analysis data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lmo4 progressively increases and co-localizes with double C/S+ neurons after birth in the somatosensory area.
source: This study also demonstrates that Lmo4 progressively increases and co-localizes with double C/S+ neurons after birth in the somatosensory area.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analysis of Lmo4 expression shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lmo4 is a widely expressed transcriptional modulator known to regulate several key biological processes, from cell growth to fate determination.
source: Lmo4 is a widely expressed transcriptional modulator known to regulate several key biological processes, from cell growth to fate determination (Sang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sang et al., 2014.

claim: Lmo4 acts as a scaffolding protein for the assembly of multi-protein complexes and interacts with several co-factors of the NuRD complex.
source: It is well known that Lmo4 acts as a scaffolding protein for the assembly of multi-protein complexes and interacts with several co-factors of the NuRD complex (Gomez-Smith et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Gomez-Smith et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007a).

claim: Lmo4 de-represses Ctip2 by sequestering Hdac1, a critical component of the NuRD complex recruited by Satb2 on the Ctip2 locus to inactivate its transcription.
source: Although other factors might be involved in Satb2/Ctip2 co-expression, our work demonstrates that Lmo4 de-represses Ctip2 by sequestering Hdac1, a critical component of the NuRD complex recruited by Satb2 on the Ctip2 locus to inactivate its transcription.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the Co-IP and ChIP data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The control of epigenetic mechanisms may underlie area-specific variations in neuronal features.
source: Overall, our data constitute first direct evidence that the control of epigenetic mechanisms may underlie area-specific variations in neuronal features.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstration that Lmo4-mediated epigenetic regulation varies across cortical areas.

claim: Epigenetic processes take place after birth and seem to contribute to the maturation and refinement rather than to the initial specification of neuronal subtypes of the somatosensory area.
source: Most importantly, such processes take place after birth and seem to contribute to the maturation and refinement rather than to the initial specification of neuronal subtypes of the somatosensory area.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal dynamics of Lmo4 expression and C/S+ cell specification occurring postnatally.

claim: Lmo4 seems to be able to induce Satb2 expression in Ctip2-positive cells.
source: Obviously, this study does not constitute an exhaustive investigation on the molecular mechanisms regulated by Lmo4, which seems to be also able to induce Satb2 expression in Ctip2-positive cells, since a notable portion of C/S+ cells seems to derive from a subpopulation of Ctip2+ cells (model in Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C/S+ cells can arise from Ctip2+ cells, as suggested by the model in Figure 8.

claim: Lmo4 expression was correlated with callosal (Satb2+) development.
source: This is not totally unexpected in light of previous reports that correlated Lmo4 expression with callosal (Satb2+) development (Azim et al., 2009; Molnar and Cheung, 2006; Ye et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Azim et al., 2009; Molnar and Cheung, 2006; Ye et al., 2015).

claim: The number of C/S+ cells decreased in Lmo4 mutants on the total of the Ctip2+ subpopulation.
source: Accordingly, we found that the number of C/S+ cells decreased in Lmo4 mutants not only on the total of the Satb2+ subpopulation but also on the total of the Ctip2+ one, suggesting that C/S+ cells may also derive from Lmo4-mediated de-repression (and/or activation) of Satb2 in Ctip2+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: C/S+ cells may derive from Lmo4-mediated de-repression (and/or activation) of Satb2 in Ctip2+ cells.
source: Accordingly, we found that the number of C/S+ cells decreased in Lmo4 mutants not only on the total of the Satb2+ subpopulation but also on the total of the Ctip2+ one, suggesting that C/S+ cells may also derive from Lmo4-mediated de-repression (and/or activation) of Satb2 in Ctip2+ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C/S+ cells decrease relative to both Satb2+ and Ctip2+ populations in Lmo4 mutants.

claim: Ctip2 was poorly upregulated in upper layers of Nr2f1 CKO motorized somatosensory cortices and of Lmo4-electroporated cortices.
source: Finally, we noticed that Ctip2 was poorly upregulated in upper layers of Nr2f1 CKO motorized somatosensory cortices and of Lmo4-electroporated cortices.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: There may be a laminar-specific transcription factor that acts synergistically with Lmo4 to efficiently activate Ctip2 expression in lower layers.
source: This could be explained by the presence of a laminar-specific transcription factor, which would act synergistically with Lmo4 to efficiently activate Ctip2 expression in lower layers.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation to explain the layer-specific effects of Lmo4.

claim: Lmo4 had been implicated in specifying SCPN and CPN identities in the rostral motor cortex.
source: Lmo4 had already been implicated in specifying SCPN and CPN identities in the rostral motor cortex (Cederquist et al., 2013), but a similar function in sensory areas was not previously unveiled.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cederquist et al., 2013.

claim: Lmo4 acts preferentially in layers V and VI of the S1 cortex in which the majority of neurons (SCPN) projects subcerebrally and expresses Ctip2 at different levels.
source: Here, we show that Lmo4 acts preferentially in layers V and VI of the S1 cortex in which the majority of neurons (SCPN) projects subcerebrally and expresses Ctip2 at different levels.
evidence: This is supported by the expression analysis and functional studies shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lmo4 levels gradually increase from layer VI to upper layers at postnatal stages, together with the progressive specification of C/S+ cells.
source: Lmo4 levels gradually increase from layer VI to upper layers at postnatal stages, together with the progressive specification of C/S+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal and laminar analysis of Lmo4 expression shown in Figure 4B.

claim: C/S+ neuron projections target the brainstem, but not the spinal cord.
source: Interestingly, we report that C/S+ neuron projections target the brainstem, but not the spinal cord.
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Ctip2 and Satb2 inhibit the expression of DCC and Unc5C, respectively, two receptors of the guidance cue Netrin-1.
source: Ctip2 and Satb2 inhibit the expression of DCC and Unc5C, respectively, two receptors of the guidance cue Netrin-1 (Srivatsa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Srivatsa et al., 2014.

claim: DCC and Unc5C are involved in the midline crossing of corticospinal axons.
source: Since these receptors are involved in the midline crossing of corticospinal axons (Finger et al., 2002), one conceivable hypothesis would be that co-expression of Ctip2 and Satb2 inhibits both receptors, thus preventing subcerberal PNs to reach the spinal cord.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Finger et al., 2002.

claim: Co-expression of Ctip2 and Satb2 may inhibit both DCC and Unc5C receptors, thus preventing subcerebral PNs to reach the spinal cord.
source: Since these receptors are involved in the midline crossing of corticospinal axons (Finger et al., 2002), one conceivable hypothesis would be that co-expression of Ctip2 and Satb2 inhibits both receptors, thus preventing subcerberal PNs to reach the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain why C/S+ neurons don't reach the spinal cord.

claim: Lmo4 might inhibit neurite outgrowth by repressing the expression of the receptor tyrosine kinase Alk.
source: Another explanation could be that Lmo4 inhibits neurite outgrowth by repressing the expression of the receptor tyrosine kinase Alk that plays key roles in neuritogenesis (Lasek et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis with citation to Lasek et al., 2011.

claim: Lmo4 might interact with Lhx2, another LIM homeobox transcription factor known to regulate the expression of the guidance receptors Ephrin-A5 as well as Robo1 and 2.
source: Alternatively, Lmo4 might interact with Lhx2, another LIM homeobox transcription factor known to regulate the expression of the guidance receptors Ephrin-A5 as well as Robo1 and 2, which in turn control different steps of corticospinal axon pathfinding (Marcos-Mondejar et al., 2012; Shetty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis with citations to Marcos-Mondejar et al., 2012 and Shetty et al., 2013.

claim: Either Lmo4 expression or Ctip2 and Satb2 co-expression might control several neuronal processes allowing the correct maturation and/or refinement of PT and IT subtypes during postnatal stages of corticogenesis.
source: Thus, either Lmo4 expression or Ctip2 and Satb2 co-expression might control several neuronal processes allowing the correct maturation and/or refinement of PT and IT subtypes during postnatal stages of corticogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the various potential mechanisms discussed.

claim: Other transcription factors normally involved in determining distinct classes of PNs during development might take a similar postnatal function during cortical maturation.
source: We envisage that also other transcription factors normally involved in determining distinct classes of PNs during development, might take a similar postnatal function during cortical maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the findings about Lmo4.

claim: Area- and time-specific changes in common molecular mechanisms modulate the final features of both CPN and SCPN subpopulations.
source: Overall, we show that area- and time-specific changes in common molecular mechanisms modulate the final features of both CPN and SCPN subpopulations in an area- and time-specific manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the findings presented in the study.

claim: A common developmental program directs the molecular and cellular maturation of both IT and PT projection neurons.
source: More in general, our analysis provides first direct evidence of a common developmental program directing the molecular and cellular maturation of both IT and PT projection neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Lmo4 affects both CPN (IT) and SCPN (PT) subpopulations.

claim: 'Serial homologies' among neocortical areas might be due to variations on a 'common theme' rather than to multiple independent and area-specific genetic programs.
source: This might have important implications in the study of neocortical development, since 'serial homologies' (i.e. similar connectivity or molecular codes) among neocortical areas might be due to variations on a 'common theme', as previously suggested (Harris and Shepherd, 2015), rather than to multiple independent and area-specific genetic programs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications of the findings, with citation to Harris and Shepherd, 2015.
